rationale:
Committed hard to flat-graphic: near-textureless colour blocking where every mass is one flat colour plus at most ONE hard-edged shadow shape. No dithering, no gradients, no wear chips, no rendering. Two global laws do all the "lighting": (1) a single hard vertical shadow split at x>=32 — everything right of that line drops one flat step; (2) the camera looks down, so every upward-facing plane (helmet crown, brim top, shoulder tops, rig top, belt, boot cuffs, boot toe-caps) gets one flat lighter band. That second rule is what sells the 2:1 dimetric down-angle without any shading.

Value hierarchy is deliberate and three-tier: the head is the brightest zone (skin + bone crown stripe + amber lenses), the coat is a big calm mid-value mass, and the ink/leather/boots are the floor. The eye lands on the head first, every time — that is the direct fix for "it looks like it's facing away."

Colour budget is a restrained triangle rather than scatter: bone appears twice (crown stripe, chest cross), amber twice (goggle lenses, injector charge), rust three times distributed top-to-bottom (goggle strap, two gauntlets, belt buckle). Metal is reserved entirely for the weapon. Deepest ink is the canon plum-black #120b10; no magenta, no chartreuse. 23 colours.

Proportions: 3.26 heads tall (head r1-r19 = 19 rows, figure r1-r62 = 62 rows), 24px-wide brim against 30px shoulders — squat and heroic, not naturalistic. Hands are 12x12 mitts, the injector is a full 35 rows of the canvas.

What it sacrifices: no material texture at all — cloth, leather and metal are told apart by hue and by hard silhouette, not by surface. The coat is a large uninflected slab up close, which will look bare next to any rendered treatment in the lineup. Fabric folds are reduced to one hem shadow. The asymmetry (weapon left, hanging fist right) means this pose will not mirror cleanly for a left-facing frame; it needs re-authoring rather than a flip.
frontFacingCue:
Three stacked cues, all of which are impossible to read as a back view. (1) The goggle band: a full-width dark housing across the head carrying two flat amber lenses split by a nose bridge, sitting under a hard-dark brim underside. It is the highest-chroma shape on the sprite and it is unmistakably a face plane. (2) Below it, four rows of bare skin — nose in shade tone, a flat ink mouth bar, a jaw that narrows to a chin — in a value that separates hard from the dark maroon hair columns flanking it and the dark helmet above. (3) The chest: a bone cross on a dark front-plane rig, an object that only exists on the front of a torso.

Head/shoulder clearance is structural, not implied. The chin ends at r19; the neck at r20-r21 is only 6px wide, so actual background is visible on BOTH sides of it; the collar at r22 is pure interior ink; shoulders do not begin until r23. The head physically clears the shoulder line with a real gap. Nothing rises above the shoulder line except the head — the injector's plunger cap tops out at r25, exactly at the shoulder, and sits at x0-x7, far outboard of the head at x14-x33, so it never competes.
smallCheck:
Honest verdict: it survives, with one loss. Downscaled nearest-neighbour to 21x28 the load-bearing reads all hold — helmet with bone crown stripe, the amber goggle band across the face (still the single strongest cue), skin jaw, bone cross on the dark rig, two rust mitts, the amber injector column on the left, dark chunky boots. The dark/light/dark rhythm of coat-hem, trousers, boots keeps the legs from collapsing into one slab.

What is lost: the neck gap closes — at 28px the head sits directly on the shoulders. It still separates, but by value only (pure-ink collar against bright skin jaw and the overhanging brim), not by visible background. Also gone: the mouth bar, the nose, the lens glints, the knuckle division on the fists, and the needle thins to a 1px thread that nearly disappears against a busy background. The bone crown stripe narrows to ~2px but survives.

Verified in grayscale at both sizes: the silhouette reads with zero hue information, and the head remains the brightest region, so the figure still turns to face you at either scale.
